Breaking the Shell

A group exercise for people trying to change something together. List what might stop the change. Then sort those barriers according to who can move them, or what you need to find out.

Allow one to two hours. One person can keep the group’s notes here. For a session on paper, use the facilitator kit and four printable cards. The original slides are also available as a PowerPoint download.

Use a change people in the room recognise. For example, ‘Someone who rings our service should only have to tell their story once.’

Notes stay in this browser. Use ‘Print / save PDF’ if you need a copy elsewhere. On a shared device, leave out personal or sensitive details.

How to ask for barriers in the room

Give everyone two minutes and a pad of sticky notes. Ask them to imagine a day when they expected the change to be working and it wasn’t. What happened? Write one possible reason on each note, then read them out. Leave room for the person who sees it differently.

1. List the barriers

Imagine it’s the day the change was due to take effect and it hasn’t happened. What got in the way? Add each person’s answers, one barrier at a time. Leave sorting until everyone has had a say.

    2. Sort and discuss the barriers

    Choose a category for each barrier. If two people put it in different places, ask what each knows about who can act. Record whatever needs checking in the action field.

    Barriers to sort

    Brick walls

    Outside the group’s authority

    The group has checked the constraint and can’t remove it in the time available. A statutory deadline is one example.

    Which part is fixed? What can we still change about how we meet it?

    Paper walls

    An assumption one person can check

    Someone says that a manager must approve every referral. Ask to see the rule or find a recent referral where another person made the decision.

    Who could check this before the group meets again?

    Partition walls

    A change that needs somebody else’s help

    Two teams want to share a rota. Changing it might take a budget decision, a change to a contract, or time from the people who draw it up.

    Who has the authority, information, or time we need?

    Mindset issues

    A belief that people have come to share

    If everyone expects a complaint to lead to blame, staff may learn to keep quiet. Inviting one person to speak up leaves the rest of the arrangement in place.

    What happens here that keeps the belief alive? What could we try together?

    3. Agree what to do next

    Read back the actions. For each one, name the person who will take it and when the group will hear back. If a barrier looks fixed, write down what you checked and how you’ll work within it. Use ‘Print / save PDF’ to take the list away.
